title: 6 GHz Wi-Fi® Sustainability Highlights
content:
Digital services generate enormous socioeconomic benefits, but they also consume energy. As user reliance on high 
bandwidth, low latency applications like augmented and virtual reality (AR/VR), cloud computing, and high definition video 
streaming continues to grow, many nations are working to curb climate change1 - meaning that connectivity must be 
reliable and sustainable. Wi-Fi® offers a dependable, energy-efficient connectivity solution, but it requires adequate 
spectrum to support an increasing number of users and devices. It is critical that spectrum policymakers allow Wi-Fi 
access to the full 6 GHz band to achieve these ambitious connectivity and sustainability goals.  
Wi-Fi and FTTH provide sustainable connectivity 
The vast majority of broadband usage occurs indoors, and 6 GHz Wi -Fi combined with fiber-to-the-home (FTTH) is the 
most practical means to deliver cost-effective, sustainable connectivity. A study by WIK-Consult for Wi-Fi Alliance® 
explored Wi-Fi and FTTH’s impact on sustainability and reported that FTTH networks are 2.5x more energy efficient per 
megabyte transmitted than 5G networks, which would need to connect an indoor device to an outdoor base station and 
penetrate building walls to support indoor connections. As such, 5G networks use a disproportionate amount of energy, 
resulting in shorter recharge cycles, increased battery wear, and additional electronic waste compared to Wi-Fi and FTTH.  
Full band 6 GHz Wi-Fi advances 
sustainability goals 
The study, Sustainability Benefits of 6 GHz Spectrum Policy,   
analyzed the effect of Wi-Fi’s access to the 6 GHz band in 
combating climate change and utilized demand models to 
compare 2 possible scenarios in Europe: 
Scenario 1: Assigning the entire 6 GHz 
band to Wi-Fi 
• With access to the full 6 GHz band, FTTH capacity is not 
constrained by a lack of spectrum for Wi-Fi 
• Models predict that making the full 6 GHz band available to 
Wi-Fi allows for sufficient spectrum to meet advanced 
indoor connectivity needs 
Scenario 2: Assigning only the upper  
6 GHz band to mobile  
• Restricting Wi-Fi’s access to the full 6 GHz band results in increased Wi-Fi congestion 
• Many consumers will not be adequately served through fixed connections, thus forcing them to utilize 5G networks 
 
 
1 2030 climate targets 
6 GHz Wi-Fi®: powering 
sustainable connections 

 
• Models predict that this could lead to a 15% shift in traffic from Wi-Fi/FTTH to mobile, resulting in a 16% increase in 
energy consumption 
The study provides clear evidence that with sufficient access to spectrum, Wi-Fi and FTTH outperform cellular networks 
in delivering broadband connectivity with significant reductions in energy consumption and environmental footprint.  
Energy consumption will increase without full access to 6 GHz 
It is crucial that adequate spectrum is made available for Wi-Fi, particularly in the full 6 GHz band. While many countries, 
including Argentina, Brazil, Canada, South Korea, and the U.S., have made the entire 6 GHz band available to Wi-Fi, the EU 
has opened less than half of the band – an insufficient amount of spectrum to meet the growing demand for high quality 
broadband connectivity in the home. 
If Europe chooses not to make the upper portion of the 6 GHz band (the 6425-7125 MHz) license-exempt, WIK-Consult 
calculated that 15% of traffic in the region would transfer from fixed to mobile networks. The study estimates that this shift 
would result in 16% higher energy consumption, leading to 3.2 megatons of additional CO2 emissions in Europe per year 
by 2030 – equivalent to the Democratic Republic of Congo’s fossil CO2 emissions in 2020.2  
Realizing the full potential of fiber depends on Wi-Fi 
The European Digital Decade Programme has set a target that by 2030 all Europeans should have access to fixed gigabit 
connectivity up to the network termination point, meaning that nearly 100% of EU households will likely be served with an 
FTTH connection.3  Furthermore, IDC Research reports an estimated 23.3 billion Wi-Fi devices in use in 2025, reflecting 
the enormous global demand for cost-effective, versatile connectivity. With an anticipated 626.9 million Wi-Fi 6E and 
583.2 million Wi-Fi 7 devices – both of which utilize the 6 GHz band for reliable, real-time performance – expected to ship 
in 2025,4 the need for access to full band 6 GHz Wi-Fi is clear.  
Policymakers must make the full 6 GHz band available to Wi-Fi  
Making the full 6 GHz band license-exempt will allow Europeans to realize the maximum potential of the advanced 
capabilities of emerging technology. Furthermore, widespread use of Wi-Fi, rather than a shift towards 5G, will help to 
reduce the environmental footprint of telecommunications networks and support Europe’s goal of becoming the world’s 
first climate-neutral continent.

1 Introduction 
Wi-Fi Protected Access (WPA) is a subset of IEEE P802.11i, IEEE Standard for 
Information Technology, Telecommunications and Information Exchange between 
systems, Local and metropolitan area networks, Specific requirements; Part 11: Wireless 
Medium Access Control (MAC) and Physical Layer (PHY) specifications: Amendment 
6: Medium Access Control (MAC) Security Enhancements, which satisfies certain 
requirements of the full IEEE P802.11i standard.   
Unless otherwise specified, all references in this document to clauses refer to the IEEE 
P802.11i standard.   
Some of the most significant Wi-Fi Protected Access features include the following: 
1. WPA supports two authenticated key management protocols in infrastructure 
mode, using 802.1X with pre-shared key and with extensible authentication 
protocol (EAP) authentication. A simple independent basic service set (IBSS) 
approach is described for reference but not supported in WPA. The IBSS 
approach described uses no authenticated key management protocol but instead a 
pre-shared key directly as the encryption/integrity key. (Note: IBSS is much 
reduced in security because it has no key management.) 
2. Access points (APs) and Stations shall use IEEE 802.11 open authentication when 
they use WPA. The 802.11 MAC state machine is the same as the existing state 
machine in Figure 8 of the IEEE 802.11 1999 (R2003) standard. 
3. APs must advertise what they support (cipher suite, authentication modes). 
Stations must request the cipher suites and authenticated key management 
protocol they want. A propriety information element in the Beacon and probe 
response messages is used to carry this information. The station uses the same 
information element in association request message. 
This is described in Section 2.1 and Appendix C. 
4. Authentication and Association are required. 
This is described in Section 2.2. 
5. Temporal key integrity protocol (TKIP) encryption with the Michael integrity 
check is required. 
TKIP and Michael are described in Section 3.3. 
6. WPA does not perform an integrity check on management and control messages. 
7. WPA does not support preauthentication for fast handoff. 
8. Management information base (MIB) support is as follows: 
Station: 
Implementations of WPA will need a configuration utility (or similar) to 
configure the pre-shared key. (This is implementation dependent and will not 
be defined here.) The pre-shared key shall be a 256bit key (because it is used 
as the pairwise master key (PMK), and the implementation will need to enter 
Version 3.1 – August 2004  
 
2
this value either as a 256bit key via hex or via an American Standard Code for 
International Interchange (ASCII) password. The key must be entered as 64 
hex characters, although entering the key in a different format may be 
possible. If the key is entered as an ASCII password, the 256bit key must be 
generated as described in Section 2.3. 
A station shall be able to configure a different pre-shared key for each service set 
identifier (SSID). 
Configuration of cipher suites is also supported. (This is implementation dependent and 
will not be defined here.)

although entering the key in a different format may be possible. If the key is

The AP control panel will also need to provide configuration for the interval

Configuration of cipher suites is also supported. (This is implementation

2 WPA Overview 
WPA supports the changes to the 1999 802.11 standard as described in the following 
clauses of IEEE P802.11i: 
• 7.1.3.1.9 
• 7.2.2 
• 7.2.3.1 
• 7.2.3.4 
• 7.2.3.6 
• 7.2.3.9 
• 7.2.3.10. 
The framework and operation of WPA are described in the following clauses: 
• 8.1 
• 8.1.1 (TKIP only) 
• 8.1.2 
• 8.1.3 
• 8.1.4 
• 8.2 (including all subsections). 
The following considerations will be useful in the development of a WPA 
implementation. 
APs advertise their capabilities in a WPA information element (IE). If the network 
administrator does not want particular ciphers to be used, then they should not be 
advertised in the WPA IE for the AP/station. APs/stations should also be capable of being 
configured to either allow/not allow non-WPA stations to associate. When configured to 
allow association of non-WPA stations, the multicast cipher shall be wired equivalent 
privacy (WEP). 
The configuration options an AP should support are as follows: 
1. Selection of one or more station configurations to associate to the AP: 
a. WPA 
b. WEP 
c. WEP rekeying by using the existing 802.1X EAP over LANs 
(EAPOL)-key message 
2. Selection of  the list for WPA of available ciphers for unicast: 
a. TKIP 
b. AES 
3. Pre-shared key for WPA that can be an ASCII passphrase or a 256bit key 
Version 3.1 – August 2004  
 
6
4. WEP key for static WEP stations that can be 40 or 104bits in length. 
The configuration options a station should support are as follows: 
1. Selection of the AP configurations the station will associate to: 
a. WPA 
b. WEP 
2. Selection of the cipher for WPA to use for unicast 
a. TKIP 
b. AES 
3. Pre-shared key for WPA that can be an ASCII passphrase or a 256bit key 
4. WEP key for static WEP stations that can be 40 or 104bits in length. 
The use of pre-shared key is recommended for home use only. When the PSK is used as 
the PMK, impersonation between stations or a station impersonating an AP is possible. 
The multicast cipher must always be the lowest unicast cipher enabled. Thus, if WEP is 
enabled in 1, then the multicast is WEP. If only WPA is enabled in 1, and TKIP is 
enabled in 2, then the multicast cipher is TKIP.  
Stations get the WPA information element from the Beacon or Probe Response messages. 
Based on the station encryption/integrity capabilities and policy configuration of the 
ciphers that the station is willing to communicate with, the station decides which APs it is 
willing to use. The policy configuration may include the ciphers that the station is willing 
to use, the authenticated key management that the station is willing to use, whether the 
station is willing to allow Group keys to be used for unicast, etc. 
If the station or AP receives a WPA information element with an authentication suite of 
WPA, then it shall perform 802.1X authentication and 802.1X key management. If the 
authentication suite is WPA-PSK, then the station or AP shall do 802.1X key 
management. 
(Note: 802.1X key management is the term used for managing the keys using IEEE 
802.1X EAPOL-Key message, as described in Section 2.2.4, with modifications as 
noted.) 
If the station does not receive a WPA information element in the Beacon or Probe 
Response, the station shall follow the normal 802.11 authentication. (This may include 
the current 802.1X authentication.) 
If the AP does not receive a WPA information element in the Association Request, the 
AP shall follow the normal 802.11 association processing. (This may include the current 
802.1X authentication.) 
(Note: The AP shall have a way to disable non-WPA clients from associating.) 
If the AP supports WPA and non-WPA stations, the following cases must be considered: 
1. The non-WPA station supports an 802.1X supplicant that is a non-WPA 802.1X 
supplicant. The AP can use 802.1X to send WEP key updates to the station. A 
Version 3.1 – August 2004  
 
7
non-WPA supplicant only supports group keys, and the AP must track per station 
whether it supports unicast keys.  
2. The non-WPA station does not support an 802.1X supplicant. The WEP key must 
be pre-configured into the non-WPA station and AP. Because the AP must use the 
pre-configured key for broadcast/multicast traffic, it must use WPA key update 
exchanges to send the key to the WPA stations. This means that the WPA stations 
in this configuration will have fixed keys for broadcast/multicast traffic, although 
they may use different keys for the unicast traffic if supported by the station and 
AP. The AP shall use WPA Group key exchange to send the fixed WEP key to 
the WPA stations. 
When WPA and non-WPA stations are both enabled, it should be possible to enter a 
default WEP key and disable group key updating to support case 2.  
By default, group key updating should be enabled, and if 802.1X is enabled on the AP, 
then 802.1X shall be used to update the group key on non-WPA stations. 
The station then associates with the AP by using an association request message. The 
association request message specifies the unicast and multicast ciphers it wants, given the 
station’s cipher capabilities and configuration. When the station receives the association 
response, it authenticates by using 802.1X with the AP. The AP sends an 802.11 
association response message (with Reason code 1) if something in the WPA information 
element was not recognized or accepted. When the AP receives the RADIUS accept, then 
the AP sends an EAP-Success to complete the authentication at the station. The AP does 
an EAPOL-Key message exchange with the station to set up the encryption/integrity keys 
with the station and sets the Secure bit in the EAPOL-Key message when the initial keys 
are sent to the station.  
(Note: In general, reference in this document to sending an 802.11 disassociation and/or 
802.11 deauthenticate message means that the 802.11 MAC sends the necessary 
messages to get to state 1 between the source and destination stations, as shown in the 
state machine diagram in Figure 8 in the IEEE 802.11 1999 standard.) 
When a station or AP fills the WPA information element, the multicast cipher is from 
multicast cipher selection, and the unicast cipher is from unicast cipher selection. If WPA 
is enabled and there is no pre-configured key, then the authenticated key management is 
WPA. Otherwise, the authenticated key management protocol is WPA-PSK if the 
station/AP is in extended service set (ESS) mode; otherwise, it is WPA-None. 
When all stations associated with an AP are 802.1X and WPA stations, and a station that 
does not use 802.1X or WPA wants to associate, the new station must use the pre-
configured key for broadcast/multicast.  The AP can use the knowledge of whether a non-
WPA station is associated to generate a multicast key with the existing stations as they 
associated until a non-WPA station wants to associate, and then send the pre-configured 
key to the existing stations (so that all stations will then be using the pre-configured key).  
Otherwise, it can send the pre-configured key to all stations as they associate. 
If the legacy station is configured to use default key 0 as the broadcast key, a WPA AP 
must use the Unicast as Group key WPA capability bit to decide whether to use Pairwise 
keys as encryption/integrity keys.

2.1 Advertisement of WPA Availability 
Advertisement of WPA availability will be done by a propriety information element in 
the beacon, probe response, association request, and re-association request messages. The 
beacon and probe response messages advertise the AP capabilities; the association 
request and re-association request messages contain the configuration that the station has

WPA uses the robust security network (RSN) Information Element described in Clause 
7.3.2.25 with the following changes: 
• The element identifier (ID) shall be 221 instead of 48. 
• An additional 4 octets shall be inserted before the Version field containing an 
organizationally unique identifier (OUI) and type fields of 00:50:F2:01. 
• The OUI shall be 00:50:F2 instead of 00:0F:AC. 
• WPA does not support counter mode with CBC-MAC protocol (CCMP); it

2.2.1 Associate/Re-Associate 
The following rules shall be applied: 
1. A station must use IEEE 802.11 open authentication. 
2. A station must complete 802.1X, and obtain and install keys before attempting to 
send class 3 data packets other than 802.1X. 
3. An AP must complete 802.1X, and obtain and install keys before attempting to 
send class 3 data packets on or off the DS for a station.   
4. If the IEEE 802.1X authentication fails, a station may try again or attempt to 
authenticate to another AP.  
5. If the AP does not have the station authenticated, it shall send a deauthenticate 
message to the station on receiving any message from that station.  
6. If the AP fails during authentication, it sends a deauthenticate message. 
7. An AP can delete a station’s state if required because of inactivity timeout, 
resource shortages, etc. This occurs if the AP wants to recover the resources used

Normally, the station and APs will send either encrypted data or unencrypted data 
packets. The only unencrypted data packets allowed are unicast 802.1X data packets; and 
unencrypted 802.1X data packets are allowed only when there is no Pairwise key 
between the station and AP. Otherwise, unencrypted data packets must be discarded. If 
the station and AP key state get out of synchronization, the following rules apply: 
2.2.2.1 AP 
If the AP receives a unicast encrypted packet that it does not have keys to decrypt, it 
should send a disassociate message to the station and discard the data packet. 
2.2.2.2 Station 
On receiving a disassociate message or an 802.11 deauthenticate message, a station 
should delete the Pairwise key and attempt to rejoin the network (i.e., reassociate to an 
AP if the station was a member of an ESS).

DISCONNECT: This state is entered as an EAPOL-Key message is received and 
fails its message integrity code (MIC) check. It sends a deauthenticate message to 
the Access Point and enters the INITIALIZE state. 
DISCONNECTED: This state is entered when disassociate or deauthenticate 
messages are received. 
INITIALIZE: This state is entered from the DISCONNECTED state, when a 
DeauthenticationRequest event occurs or when the station initializes. The state 
initializes the key state variables. 
AUTHENTICATION: This state is entered when an AuthentiationRequest is sent 
from the Management entity to authentication a BSSID. 
AUTHENTICATION2: This state is entered from the AUTHENTICATION state or 
from the PTKINITDONE state. 
INITPMK: This state is entered when the 802.1X backend authentication server 
completes successfully. If supplied, a RadiusKey goes to the PTKSTART state; 
otherwise, it goes to the DISCONNECTED state.  
INITPSK: This state is entered when a pre-shared key is configured. 
PTKSTART: This state is entered from INITPMK or INITPSK to start the 4-way 
handshake, or if no response to the 4-way handshake occurs. 
PTKINITNEGOTIATING: This state is entered when the second EAPOL-Key 
message for the 4-way handshake is received with the key type of Pairwise key. 
PTKINITDONE: This state is entered when the last EAPOL-Key message for the 4-
way handshake is received with the key type of Pairwise key. This state may call 
SetPTK. If this call fails, the AP shall detect and recover from the situation (for 
example, by performing a Disconnect event for this association). 
UPDATEKEYS: This state is entered when an EAPOL-Key message is received 
from the Supplicant to initiate the 4-way handshake from the Supplicant. The key 
type in the EAPOL-Key message must be set to Pairwise key, and the Request bit 
must be set. 
INTEGRITYFAILURE: This state is entered when a data integrity failure occurs either 
locally or from a remote station by receiving an EAPOL-Key message with the key 
type set to Pairwise key. The Request and Error bits must be set.

3.1 Active Countermeasures  
MIC countermeasures are as described in Clause 8.3.2.3.2, except that upon a subsequent 
MIC failure within 60 seconds, the behavior is as follows: 
When a subsequent MIC failure occurs within 60 seconds of the preceding failure, then a 
device will disassociate itself (if a Supplicant) or disassociate all associated STAs (if an 
Authenticator).  Furthermore, the device will not deliver any class 3 TKIP encrypted data 
frames to or from any peer for a period of 60 seconds. If the device is an AP, it shall 
disallow new associations for a period of 60 seconds; at the end of the 60-second period, 
the AP shall resume normal operations and allow STAs to (re)associate.  If the device is a 
Supplicant, it shall first send a Michael MIC failure report frame prior to revoking its 
PTK and disassociation. 
The countermeasures used by an Authenticator are depicted in Figure 4 and described as 
follows: 
• For an Authenticator that detects a Michael MIC failure event: 
1. Increment the MIC failure counter. 
2. If this is the first MIC failure, initialize the countermeasures timer.  If the 
failure was in a unicast frame, discard the offending frame. 
3. If less than 60 seconds have passed since a previous Michael MIC failure, 
transition every STA using TKIP (for either unicast or broadcast/multicast 
frames) in the BSS to State 2 in the 802.11 state diagram. This effectively 
disassociates and deletes the PTK for all the STAs.  The group temporal key 
(GTK) must also be revoked.  The Authenticator shall disallow associations 
using TKIP for the duration of 60 seconds. At the end of the 60 seconds, the 
MIC failure counter and timer may be reset, and new associations resume.  
4. If the Authenticator is using EAP, transition the state of the Authenticator 
state machine to State INITIALIZE.  This will restart the EAP state machine.  
If the Authenticator is using PSKs, this step is omitted.

3.3 TKIP and Michael Implementation Checklist 
Carrying out the following checklist has been found to be useful in validating the TKIP 
and Michael implementations: 
1. The TKIP and MIC engines are verified against the test vectors. 
2. The MIC is calculated on the MSDU and not the MPDU fragments. 
3. The two addresses that are MICed with the data portion of the MSDU are 
destination address (DA) and source address (SA), the ultimate destination and 
source of the packet, and not the transmitter address (TA) and receiver address 
(RA). (Note: The DA and SA are in different positions of the 802.11 header, 
depending on whether sent to or from the AP.) 
4. The MIC key used on the Client for transmit (TX) is in bytes 24–31, and the MIC 
key used on the Client for receive (RX) is in bytes 16–23 of the PTK. 
That is, assume that TX MIC and RX MIC referred to in Clause 8.7 are 
referenced to the Authenticator.  Similarly, on the AP, the MIC used for TX is in 
bytes 16–23, and the MIC key used for RX is in bytes 24–31 of the PTK. 
5. The MSDU is padded with a byte of 0x5a and then from 4 to 7 0x00s before 
calculating the MIC on TX.  (Variable padding ensures that MIC is calculated on 
a multiple of 4-byte words.) 
6. The pad bytes in 5. are not transmitted with the packet.  That is, the 8 byte MIC is 
inserted after the last byte of the original payload. 
7. On RX, a pad byte of 0x5a and from 4–7 bytes of 0x00 is inserted between the 
last byte of data and the MIC, and included in the MIC calculation.  The MIC 
itself in the RX frame is not part of the MIC calculation but is compared to the 
MIC calc output. 
8. The pad bytes inserted in the packet on RX are not sent up to Windows with the 
packet. 
9. The TKIP Phase 1 calculation uses the Transmitter Address.  A client uses its own 
address for TX P1k and the AP's Address for RX P1K.

initializing the TSC to 0's, then the P1K must be run on the 0's TSC before the

11. The IV inserted into the TX Packet conforms to the coding described in the WPA

title: Wi-Fi 7 and education: Unlocking a new era of digital learning
content:
Walk into any modern classroom today, and you'll see a world that looks nothing like it did a decade ago. Students aren't just reading from textbooks—they're streaming high-definition videos, joining virtual field trips, collaborating on cloud-based projects, and engaging with digital tools that bring subjects to life. Learning has become more dynamic, more interactive, and more dependent on fast, reliable connectivity.
But while the tools have evolved, many school networks haven’t, as made evident by dropped connections during live lessons, slow-buffering videos, and large file sizes that are difficult to download. The need for stronger, smarter wireless infrastructure has never been clearer.
That’s where
Wi-Fi 7
steps in—not just as a technical upgrade, but to enable the learning experiences today’s education demands.
Wi-Fi 7 is a game changer for education
Wi-Fi 7 isn’t just a technical leap; it’s an enabler of richer, more interactive learning experiences. With advancements like higher data efficiency through 4K-QAM, the low latency of Multi-Link Operation (MLO), and superwide channels of the 6 GHz band
[1]
, schools and universities can finally match their network performance to the demands of today’s digital classrooms. This means glitch-free 4K streaming for virtual lectures, real-time collaboration on cloud projects, and seamless access to large multimedia resources — no more dropped connections or lag disrupting lessons.
More importantly, this next-generation connectivity empowers institutions to adopt immersive extended reality (XR) tools, personalized learning platforms, and hybrid models at scale. Teachers gain the freedom to integrate advanced instructional aids without worrying about bandwidth limits, while students can confidently engage in dynamic, collaborative activities both in the classroom and remotely. By delivering faster speeds, ultra-low latency, and robust reliability, Wi-Fi 7 ensures that technology fades into the background so educators can stay focused on teaching.
Performance improvements users can depend on
In educational settings, we're seeing download speeds that are 3-5x faster than Wi-Fi 6, enabling instant access to learning resources even for very large files. However, speed is just the beginning of the story. Perhaps the most significant feature for educational environments is the dramatic reduction in latency — down to 1-2 milliseconds in optimal conditions
[2]
— which helps eliminate the lag that often disrupts virtual classrooms and interactive learning applications. Connection reliability also improves with early Wi-Fi 7 deployments
[3]
reporting up to a 35% reduction in dropped connections, particularly in high-density environments like lecture halls. Additionally, Wi-Fi 7's higher spectral efficiency and multi-user resource allocation methods allow classrooms to simultaneously support dozens of bandwidth-intensive applications without performance degradation. A teacher can stream 4K instructional videos while students participate in virtual labs, attend remote lectures, and collaborate on cloud documents – all on the same network with consistent performance
[4]
.
AI, immersive learning and the need for smarter connectivity
Education today is shifting from static textbooks to intelligent, immersive experiences powered by artificial intelligence (AI) and extended reality. Personalized learning platforms now use AI to adapt in real-time to each student's needs, analyzing interaction patterns and performance to deliver tailored instruction. Simultaneously, automated and virtual technologies (AR/VR) are enabling hands-on, experiential learning — from virtual dissection in biology labs to collaborative 3D modeling in engineering and real-time historical site explorations in geography.
These advancements, while transformative, are only as effective as the networks that power them. Ultra-low latency and high bandwidth are essential to support real-time feedback loops in AI and smooth, motion-synced visuals in VR, meaning Wi-Fi 7’s speed, reliability, and latency are pivotal to delivering the performance needed to make immersive learning experiences a practical, seamless component of everyday education.
IT and academic partnerships are crucial to planning network upgrades
There has been a strategic shift in how educational institutions approach network infrastructure investments. Rather than viewing connectivity as a utility cost to be minimized, forward-thinking institutions now see it as a foundational investment that directly impacts educational outcomes.
Many universities and K-12 systems are adopting multi-year technology roadmaps that prioritize
scalable network infrastructure
capable of supporting not just current needs but anticipated requirements within the next three to five years, which entails planning for Wi-Fi 7 deployment even before complete device ecosystem adoption.
Interestingly, there has also been an increased level of collaboration between IT departments and academic leadership in these investment decisions. Technology directors are being invited into curriculum planning discussions to ensure that network capabilities align with educational goals. This integrated approach represents a maturation in how educational technology is perceived — not as separate from the educational mission, but as an integral enabler of innovation in teaching and learning. As noted in Huron Consulting Group’s insights on higher education strategy,
“Strong collaboration across financial and academic leadership with IT offices is one of the key characteristics of an institution that manages data well and uses it to empower forward motion.”
[5]
Beyond 2025: Shaping the future of learning with Wi-Fi 7, AI, and beyond
As we look beyond 2025, a powerful convergence of Wi-Fi 7, AI, and upcoming Wi-Fi 8 will redefine how education is delivered and experienced.
In this next era, connectivity won’t just keep up with innovation — it will help shape it. Hyper-personalized learning paths, global virtual campuses, and seamless collaboration will become the norm, unconstrained by bandwidth or latency. The real measure of success will be technology so seamless, it disappears into the background—empowering educators and learners alike to focus on what truly matters: unlocking human potential without limits.

In November 2024, Wi-Fi Alliance® and Faculty of Medicine Ramathibodi Hospital, Mahidol University 
completed a seven-month pilot showcasing the value of full band 6 GHz Wi-Fi® in healthcare. Conducted in 
collaboration with member partners Hewlett Packard Enterprise, Intel, and Meta, the pilot successfully 
demonstrated 6 GHz Wi-Fi’s potential to revolutionize healthcare by enabling cutting-edge technologies that 
enhance patient care and operational efficiencies in dense environments.  
6 GHz Wi-Fi is vital to the future of healthcare 
The 6 GHz band brings significant benefits to healthcare by providing 
uncongested superwide 320 MHz channels and ultra-low latency 
that enables real-time patient monitoring, seamless transmission of 
large medical files, and immersive augmented and virtual reality 
(AR/VR) medical training. Despite these benefits, access to 6 GHz 
spectrum varies across global regulations, preventing some countries 
from realizing its full potential. 
The pilot’s primary goals were to demonstrate the transformative 
impact of 6 GHz Wi-Fi in high-performance, low-latency healthcare 
applications and underscore the importance of making the full band 
available for license-exempt technologies in Thailand. Two key use 
cases were tested:  
• The efficient use of AR/VR technologies for medical training in a classroom setting 
• Dense deployment, allowing every individual in a 500-seat classroom to stream HD video or utilize  
multi-layer network segmentation  
A demonstration that tested these scenarios using three 160 MHz channels (lower 500 MHz of the 6 GHz 
band) versus seven 160 MHz channels (full 1200 MHz) confirmed that full band access is essential for meeting 
the stringent performance demands of these advanced use cases.  
Superior performance demands full band 6 GHz  
The data collected during the pilot highlighted the importance of effectively utilizing all seven 160 MHz 
channels in the full 6 GHz band. Results showed that full band 6 GHz Wi-Fi delivered: 
• 2X increase in network data throughput compared to 
using only the lower 500 MHz of the 6 GHz band 
• 5X reduction in network latency, ensuring real-time 
responsiveness for mission-critical applications 
• 3X increase in user experience satisfaction ratings 
among students and faculty members

Why choose Wi-Fi for IoT?

After 25 years of innovation, Wi-Fi offers unmatched security, interoperability, and backward compatibility, making it the preferred choice for IoT applications, from smart home devices to industrial automation. Wi-Fi Alliance®’s comprehensive brochure,
Wi-Fi CERTIFIED® for IoT: Solutions for a Robust, Interoperable IoT Ecosystem

Extended range

Robust security

Seamless interoperability
: Wi-Fi CERTIFIED ensures devices from diverse vendors interoperate, minimizing support challenges and enhancing user satisfaction
Scalability
: advanced standards like Wi-Fi 6 and Wi-Fi 7 support dense networks common in IoT deployments
Global compatibility and cost

Overcoming IoT connectivity challenges
Designing IoT devices requires navigating complex connectivity decisions. Without reliable connectivity, IoT devices fail to deliver on their promises of security, efficiency, and sustainability. Key considerations include:
Network topology
: support for traditional access point/client, mesh, or peer-to-peer configurations to suit varied use cases
Simplified provisioning
: user-friendly onboarding for consumers
Power optimization
: features like Target Wake Time (TWT) extend battery life for devices like smart sensors or door locks
Wi-Fi HaLow™ is tailored for IoT excellence
Wi-Fi HaLow, operating in sub-1 GHz bands, redefines IoT connectivity. With channel widths as low as 1 MHz, it offers long-range communication, low power consumption, and superior signal penetration. Wi-Fi HaLow increases Wi-Fi range to 1 kilometer (km) or more while maintaining data rates of 150 Kbps.
Because it operates in sub-1 GHz frequency bands, Wi-Fi HaLow uses relatively “clean” spectrum, limiting the risk of interference from other devices. Capable of supporting over 8,000 devices on a single access point, Wi-Fi HaLow is ideal for smart homes, precision agriculture, and Industrial IoT (IIoT), delivering reliable performance in dense and challenging environments.
Solutions for success

Wi-Fi EasyMesh™
: extends network coverage through a unified, self-optimizing mesh of access points, ensuring consistent performance across large areas
Wi-Fi Location™
: provides sub-meter accuracy for indoor positioning, enabling applications like asset tracking, navigation, and geo-fencing while prioritizing data privacy
Matter
: as a central ingredient of Matter certification, Wi-Fi CERTIFIED ensures seamless interoperability across IP-based devices, fostering a unified IoT ecosystem through a common application layer

The IoT landscape is evolving rapidly, driven by advancements in artificial intelligence (AI) and edge computing. Wi-Fi Alliance is at the forefront, developing innovations in dynamic network management, enhanced security, and low-power operation to meet future demands. This overview only scratches the surface of Wi-Fi’s transformative role in IoT.

title: Wi-Fi CERTIFIED®: Future-proofing enterprise networks
content:
Wi-Fi® is the backbone of enterprise connectivity. From office complexes to sprawling campuses and hospitals, Wi-Fi fuels the mission-critical applications that keep businesses running. But today’s enterprise is evolving faster than ever before — and so are its connectivity requirements. As the pace of digital transformation accelerates, enterprises are facing new challenges that require more sophisticated, secure, and scalable Wi-Fi solutions.
Wi-Fi enables a new era of enterprise networking
The growing demand for cloud-based services, distributed workforces, and connected devices is putting new pressures on enterprise networks. With a projected 20% compound annual growth rate in enterprise networking equipment and more than 747 million shipments expected by 2027,
[1]
enterprise networks must deliver increased performance and security
.
Several powerful trends are reshaping connectivity in the enterprise landscape:
Reliance on the cloud
: with workloads moving to the cloud, enterprise networks must support faster, more reliable data transmission as even minor lags can disrupt business operations or halt production lines
Remote and distributed workforces
: today’s employees connect from home offices, satellite branches, or on the go, often using bandwidth-intensive apps like video conferencing and augmented and virtual reality (AR/VR)
Proliferation of devices
: today’s enterprise supports a vast array of endpoints, including laptops, smartphones, security cameras, IoT sensors, and even medical equipment, each with unique connectivity needs
Security at the forefront
: cyberattacks are becoming more frequent and more costly, with the average breach now topping $4.88 million.
[2]
As “bring your own device” (BYOD) and Internet of Things (IoT) adoption continues to grow, network security must evolve to protect both legacy and modern devices
Complex device lifecycles
: while Wi-Fi infrastructure may refresh every 3-5 years, many devices, particularly in healthcare settings, may remain in service for as long as 15 years. It is critical that enterprise networks are able to balance performance and backward compatibility for the long haul
Enterprise connectivity challenges
Wi-Fi equipment makers, service providers, and systems integrators face a host of unique challenges as they design and deploy solutions for enterprise environments. Today’s enterprise networks must support:
Interoperability:
due to an increasingly varied array of endpoint devices across multiple vendors
Backward compatibility:
networks must connect devices with multiple generations of Wi-Fi
Security:
devices and networks must be equipped to protect an organization and its customers against cyberattacks
Performance:
low latency is essential for many business-critical applications as even brief delays can affect productivity — a challenge that will only intensify as more enterprises implement AI applications
Minimal network congestion:
enterprise networks are uniquely dense due in part to a large volume of users and high peak upload and download traffic
Wi-Fi CERTIFIED drives enterprise success
In Wi-Fi’s 25 year history,
Wi-Fi CERTIFIED®
has played an essential role in accelerating the technology’s adoption by helping to ensure reliability, security, and interoperability among Wi-Fi devices. As connectivity needs continue to evolve, Wi-Fi CERTIFIED  delivers the high-performance, scalable  solutions enterprise demands.
Wi-Fi CERTIFIED 6® & Wi-Fi CERTIFIED 7™:
the latest Wi-Fi generations operate in the 2.4 GHz, 5 GHz, and 6 GHz bands to support high bandwidth, low latency applications in dense environments
Wi-Fi QoS Management™:
allows enterprise networks to prioritize traffic flows for time-sensitive services like video and telepresence
WPA3™:
provides cutting-edge security protocols to safeguard data and protect against threats
Wi-Fi Enhanced Open™:
preserves the convenience of open networks while minimizing risk
Wi-Fi Location™:
delivers accurate location information to enable indoor navigation and asset tracking
Passpoint®:
enables streamlined authentication for seamless connectivity between Wi-Fi networks and mobile devices
Wi-Fi Device Metrics:
provides a framework for device performance across diverse use cases to help IT managers and network architects better evaluate client devices for a superior experience
Discover the full potential of Wi-Fi in enterprise
Enterprise networks are only as strong as the technology behind them. As the connectivity landscape continues to evolve, Wi-Fi Alliance® will continue to drive technology advancements and solutions that ensure Wi-Fi remains the first choice for enterprise.

title: Powering a connected world: Wi-Fi® momentum in 2025
content:
A leader in connectivity
Wi-Fi® remains a fundamental component of wireless connectivity. 3.9 billion Wi-Fi devices are expected to ship in 2025, bringing total Wi-Fi shipments to 48.8 billion over the technology’s lifetime.
[1]
Currently, 23.3 billion Wi-Fi devices are in use,
[2]
found in homes with security cameras and voice assistants, enterprises with wireless printers and video conferencing systems, and industrial settings with automated machinery and sensors. Both inside and outside the home, users spend 77 - 88% of their screen-on time connected to Wi-Fi while using a smartphone,
[3]
underscoring Wi-Fi’s significance in daily life.
6 GHz Wi-Fi: Enhancing capabilities
The adoption of 6 GHz unlicensed spectrum for Wi-Fi has improved the technology’s performance, offering higher data rates, lower latency, and better reliability. Utilized by Wi-Fi 6E and Wi-Fi 7, this additional spectrum supports applications like extended reality (XR), ultra-high definition video streaming, and Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT). As of 2025, 12 countries have unlocked the entire 6 GHz band for Wi-Fi use, enabling broader access to these cutting-edge use cases. 6 GHz devices have gained traction, with 583.2 million Wi-Fi 7 devices and 626.9 million Wi-Fi 6E devices projected to ship this year.
[4]
Over 2,000 6 GHz devices have achieved Wi-Fi CERTIFIED® status, up 22% from the end of last year, indicating market demand for certified Wi-Fi products.
Growth across sectors
Wi-Fi’s significance is evident across various industries, based on 2025 shipment forecasts:
Networking:
81.6 million Wi-Fi 6E access points (APs) and 98.7 million Wi-Fi 7 APs are expected to ship, strengthening network infrastructure
[5]
Automotive:
97.5 million Wi-Fi products will support vehicle systems, including diagnostics and over-the-air (OTA) updates
[6]
Healthcare:
76.4 million Wi-Fi devices will be used in areas like telemedicine and medical equipment
[7]
IoT:
1.6 billion Wi-Fi IoT devices will ship, contributing to connected homes, cities, and industries
[8]
These numbers indicate Wi-Fi’s steady integration into multiple market segments. Beyond shipments, Wi-Fi is projected to contribute $4.9 trillion USD to the global economy in 2025,
[9]
highlighting its broader economic significance.
Reflecting on strong progress
Wi-Fi has remained relevant by continuously evolving its standards and testing processes to meet changing technology needs. Efforts like Wi-Fi CERTIFIED ensure devices meet performance and interoperability benchmarks, supporting a high-quality, reliable user experience. The technology’s ability to adapt to varying network demands — whether in dense urban areas or remote locations — contributes to its overall value. As connectivity needs shift, Wi-Fi’s ongoing enhancements position it to handle future challenges and support new opportunities.

title: 6 GHz Wi-Fi®: 5 years of unparalleled wireless innovation
content:
Five years ago, the Federal Communications Commission’s (FCC)
landmark decision
to make Wi-Fi® available to 6 GHz spectrum opened the door to unprecedented innovation and unlocked billions of dollars in economic value. To commemorate this important milestone, we spoke with Alex Roytblat, Vice President of Worldwide Regulatory Affairs at Wi-Fi Alliance®, for more insight on how 6 GHz Wi-Fi catalyzed advancements in wireless connectivity and what’s ahead for the future.
As we reflect on the past five years, what do you see as the most significant development for Wi-Fi in the 6 GHz band?
Over the past five years, the most significant development for Wi-Fi in the 6 GHz band has been the global regulatory momentum to open this spectrum for unlicensed use, starting with the FCC’s landmark decision in April 2020. That decision catalyzed a
wave of similar regulatory actions in other countries
, allowing 6 GHz Wi-Fi technology to develop and deliver multigigabit, low-latency connectivity on a scale never before possible. In parallel, the rapid integration of 6 GHz Wi-Fi radios into devices – from smartphones and laptops to enterprise-grade APs – demonstrates strong industry alignment and validates the commercial viability of 6 GHz Wi-Fi. This combination of regulatory progress and ecosystem readiness has fundamentally redefined what's possible for Wi-Fi, especially in high-density and performance-critical environments.
What do you think is the most underrated innovation to come out of opening the 6 GHz band to Wi-Fi? What's the most overhyped?
The most underrated innovation from opening the 6 GHz band to Wi-Fi is the enablement of deterministic, low-latency performance in dense environments – especially through the broader adoption of
Wi-Fi 7's scheduling and multi-link capabilities
. These advanced features are quietly transforming Wi-Fi from a best-effort technology into a serious contender for real-time, high-reliability applications like augmented and virtual reality (AR/VR), industrial automation, and telemedicine.
The most overhyped aspect is the narrative that 6 GHz Wi-Fi alone will instantly revolutionize user experiences. While the spectrum is critical, its benefits are only fully realized with corresponding ecosystem advancements – such as support in client devices, upgrades to infrastructure, and deployment in environments that actually need the extra bandwidth. Without those pieces in place, the raw spectrum alone doesn't solve congestion or deliver gigabit speeds by default.
What are some of the biggest opportunities for developers and device makers as 6 GHz Wi-Fi becomes more widespread?
As 6 GHz Wi-Fi becomes more widespread, developers and device makers are positioned to unlock entirely new classes of user experiences. With access to wider channels and lower interference, there’s room to design for real-time, high-bandwidth applications – think untethered AR/VR, cloud gaming, 8K streaming, and AI-powered assistants that rely on rapid edge-to-cloud interactions.
For developers, this means pushing the envelope on apps that demand consistent low latency and high throughput, especially in education, healthcare, industrial IoT, and immersive media. There's also an opportunity to optimize multi-link operation and adaptive connectivity strategies that take full advantage of 6 GHz performance.
For device makers, the ability to differentiate with next-generation Wi-Fi performance – whether through better thermal design, antenna systems, or software optimization – creates a competitive advantage. And as
Automated Frequency Coordination (AFC) enables outdoor use
, we’ll also see growth in W-Fi devices tailored for smart cities, outdoor mesh networks, and rural broadband.
Not all countries have made the 6 GHz band available to Wi-Fi. What is the impact on users in countries where the full 6 GHz band is not available?
In countries where the full 6 GHz band isn’t available to Wi-Fi, users are at a significant disadvantage, both in terms of performance and access to innovation. Devices may technically support advanced features like Wi-Fi 6E or Wi-Fi 7, but without the full band, they can’t deliver the wide 160 or 320 MHz channels that enable multi-gigabit speeds and ultra-low latency. This impacts everything from everyday connectivity – like streaming, gaming, and video conferencing – to more transformational use cases such as AR/VR or edge-AI solutions in education, telemedicine, and smart manufacturing. In short, users are stuck with congested legacy bands while others are moving into a new era of wireless connectivity. Moreover, the global tech ecosystem is rapidly standardizing around 6 GHz Wi-Fi. When a country lags in spectrum availability, it risks creating a digital divide – not just internally, but in terms of international competitiveness, access to next-gen applications, and alignment with global supply chains. The opportunity cost of delay is real and growing.
Looking towards the future of wireless connectivity, how do you think 6 GHz Wi-Fi will continue to fuel innovation? What are some of the most impactful advancements you foresee in the next few years?
Looking ahead, 6 GHz Wi-Fi will be a foundational enabler for the next wave of innovation across multiple sectors. With the clean, wide channels it provides, we’ll see continued growth in high-throughput, low-latency applications, especially immersive technologies like AR/VR/XR, real-time collaboration tools, and AI-driven edge computing.
One of the most impactful advancements will be the broader deployment of Wi-Fi 7, which leverages features like Multi-link Operation (MLO), 320 MHz channels, and deterministic latency to unlock use cases that were previously out of reach for Wi-Fi. This will make wireless truly viable for mission-critical enterprise, healthcare, and industrial environments. On the infrastructure side, AFC will open the door for standard power outdoor Wi-Fi, dramatically expanding coverage and enabling fiber-like performance in suburban and rural areas, helping to bridge the digital divide with lower-cost solutions. In short, 6 GHz Wi-Fi isn’t just keeping pace with innovation – it’s setting the stage for it.

title: Wi-Fi Alliance® welcomes introduction of budget reconciliation text
content:
Austin, TX and Washington, D.C. – May 12, 2025 –
Wi-Fi Alliance® commends Chairman Brett Guthrie and the House Committee on Energy and Commerce for introducing the budget reconciliation text. This legislative initiative represents a positive step toward strengthening the United States’ communications infrastructure and ensuring continued spectrum innovation.
We are especially encouraged that the bill explicitly excludes the 5.925–7.125 GHz frequency range. This provision is vital to preserving unlicensed access to the entire 6 GHz band — a foundational resource for the future of Wi-Fi technology.  By providing much-needed regulatory clarity, the bill encourages continued investment and innovation in next-generation Wi-Fi technologies, which are already delivering transformative benefits to consumers, enterprises, and public institutions.
The Communications Subtitle of the bill reaffirms Congress's recognition of the central role unlicensed spectrum plays in powering connectivity, enabling economic growth, and supporting key national priorities such as education, telehealth, and small business competitiveness.
Wi-Fi Alliance looks forward to continued collaboration with policymakers to ensure that U.S. spectrum policy keeps pace with the evolving demands of a wireless-first world.

title: Wi-Fi Alliance® commemorates landmark 6 GHz decision

Transformational spectrum decision catalyzed unprecedented innovation and connectivity advancements
Austin, Texas – April 23, 2025
– Wi-Fi Alliance® proudly marks the fifth anniversary of the U.S. Federal Communications Commission’s (FCC)
landmark decision
to open the 6 GHz band for unlicensed use, a pivotal milestone that continues to fuel innovation and connectivity through Wi-Fi®. This bold April 2020 decision unlocked billions of dollars in economic value, positioned the U.S. as a global leader in unlicensed spectrum policy, and catalyzed international momentum toward enabling a next-generation Wi-Fi® ecosystem worldwide.
The 6 GHz band has played a critical role in enabling next-generation Wi-Fi – driving the global rollout of Wi-Fi 7 – by relieving network congestion and expanding high-performance connectivity. Since the FCC’s ruling, billions of 6 GHz Wi-Fi devices have entered the market, underscoring the rapid adoption and far-reaching benefits of forward-looking spectrum policy.
"The FCC’s visionary action to open the full 6 GHz band was a pivotal moment for Wi-Fi connectivity and digital transformation globally," said Kevin Robinson, President and CEO of Wi-Fi Alliance. "Five years on, that leadership continues to drive global spectrum policy, as regulators around the world empower consumers and enterprises with Wi-Fi innovation.”
Wi-Fi Alliance is proud of the critical role we've played at the forefront of advancing 6 GHz Wi-Fi, working tirelessly to support policymakers and industry innovators. As we look ahead, we remain committed to driving further progress in spectrum policy and fostering global connectivity through continued leadership in Wi-Fi advancements.

title: Unlocking the power of collaboration: Interoperability Event highlights from Tokyo
content:
Earlier this year, Wi-Fi Alliance® hosted its 2025 Asia Member Meeting in Tokyo, Japan, bringing together industry leaders and innovators to discuss the latest advancements in Wi-Fi®. A standout session from the event was the panel on
Interoperability Events
— critical gatherings where Wi-Fi Alliance members test the functionality and compatibility of their Wi-Fi products in real-world scenarios. These events are more than just technical exercises; they are a cornerstone of the collaboration that drives the Wi-Fi ecosystem forward.
In this blog, we have distilled the panel’s rich discussion, offering a glimpse into how Interoperability Events take shape, their impact on the industry, and what is on the horizon for 2025.
How Interoperability Events come to life
The panel kicked off with Peng Yan, Wireless Technologist at Wi-Fi Alliance and primary point of contact for Interoperability Events, walking through the anatomy of an Interoperability Event. These events come in two formats: member-driven and staff-driven.
Member-driven events:
An example of these would be Interoperability Events focused on Wi-Fi HaLow™ and Wi-Fi Location™. Here, members take the lead, organizing the testing themselves while staff provide logistical support — venues, network cables, and whatever else is needed to make it happen.
Staff-driven events:
These start with a clear objective, often sparked by member feedback. For instance, when operators flagged roaming as a persistent pain point, Wi-Fi Alliance responded with a series of dedicated roaming events. Similarly, Internet of Things (IoT) devices that run on batteries require low-power functionality, prompting an event for testing interoperability with different power saving modes. This event helped Wi-Fi Alliance improve its Power Saving Features certification.
Staff identify the event’s theme, utilize testing labs like RDL in Santa Clara or collaborate with Authorized Test Labs (ATLs) worldwide, and brainstorm test scenarios with members. From there, it is all about logistics — simulating environments (such as office or home setups) and running pre-event calls with vendors to align on test scenarios. During the event week, participants execute tests, collect data, and share feedback to refine future events.
The numbers tell the story
Since September 2023, Wi-Fi Alliance has hosted Interoperability Events with more than 100 member companies participating, testing more than 450 end-product devices (not just reference designs). Gaurav Jain, VP of Technology at Wi-Fi Alliance, highlighted a key goal: doubling participation to amplify the industry-wide benefits.
“Interoperability is not just about technology — it is about collaboration,” Gaurav noted, echoing a recurring theme. These events bring together a diverse set of stakeholders — including device manufacturers, OS vendors, enterprise solution providers, and operators — to evaluate products and device implementations in deployment-relevant environments. They provide a collaborative platform to uncover compatibility issues, bridge gaps across the ecosystem, and ensure that Wi-Fi continues to deliver on its promise of seamless, reliable connectivity.
Real-world impact: Voices from the panel
The panelists shared how these events have shaped their work:
Mark Hamilton, Networking Standards Director, RUCKUS Networks:
“We passed all the tests quite easily, but not to the level of performance that we expected or wanted, and we used the Interoperability Events to solve that problem and take the next step beyond what the test cases require.” Mark emphasized the importance of working through MLO operations and behavior during the Wi-Fi 7 events, going further than what is possible during plugfests.
David Halasz, VP of Standards, Morse Micro:
Reflecting on a recent Wi-Fi HaLow event, David emphasized that even though they had to scale back activities to focus on certification testing due to spectrum constraints, “the important thing was that we were in China, and it was definitely the Interoperability Event that gave us an opportunity to perform outreach.”
Dorothy Stanley, HPE Fellow, Aruba:
“Without the Interoperability Event, we would not have had client vendors in one place to test efficiently, find the errors, and then go back and incorporate that into our implementation.” Dorothy also traced the evolution of Wi-Fi Location testing, noting how Interoperability Events have driven sub-meter accuracy and improved vendor implementations since 2018.
Guoqi Cui, Senior Test Engineer, Google:
Guoqi shared a specific Wi-Fi 7 debugging win, where an event revealed a fast-roaming conflict affecting MLO with enterprise access points. “What we found is that for an enterprise system, normally people enable fast roaming, so we discovered that the issue is really caused by that flag.”
To add to the experiences of the rest of the panel, Peng recounted how testing at a WPA3™ event shaped the compatibility mode solution, now an important part of the WPA3 program: “We had transition mode issues with many devices, so at the WPA3 event, we tested two solutions — compatibility mode (RSN Override) and multiple BSSIDs under one SSID — across over 100 devices. The goal was to ensure legacy devices could connect while newer ones used WPA3. Results led to the adoption of RSN Override, with compatibility mode launching last year to fix transition mode problems.”
Looking ahead: The Interoperability Lab and 2025 plans
Exciting developments are on the horizon. Wi-Fi Alliance is building an Interoperability Lab at RDL in Santa Clara, set to open to members in 2025. With 15+ Wi-Fi 6/Wi-Fi 7 routers, 130+ client devices (laptops, smartphones, smart home, etc.), and multiple ISP backhauls, it is designed for stringent testing of real-world scenarios.
For 2025, confirmed events include:
Wi-Fi Location
: April 28 – May 2 ∙ Santa Clara
Security
: May 5 – May 9 ∙ Santa Clara & Taipei; May 12 – May 16 ∙ Beijing
Wi-Fi 6 and Wi-Fi 7
: September 8 – September 12 ∙ Santa Clara, Taipei, and Beijing
Why Interoperability Events matter
The panel underscored that interoperability testing is not just about passing a checklist — it is about ensuring Wi-Fi works for everyone, everywhere. It also highlighted that there is no one-solution-fits-all approach to interoperability; effective testing must account for diverse needs of devices, networks, and real-world deployment scenarios. From fixing roaming issues to boosting Wi-Fi 7 performance, these events shape standards, inform certifications, and strengthen the foundation of an ever-evolving Wi-Fi ecosystem.
Interoperability Insights
, a new Wi-Fi Alliance publication for members, details actionable insights from Interoperability Events, offering significant value to members and the broader industry, even for those who did not participate in an event. With the new lab and multiple events scheduled for 2025, there has never been a better time to get involved.
